notes: Dipole Moment Workbench problem library. Each problem: id, name, formula, smiles (Lewis structure as SMILES, all non-zero formal charges explicit), type (inorganic | organic), level (1-3), mu (experimental gas-phase dipole, D; 0 for molecules with no net dipole), note (optional, shown after Step 3). Bond-moment table: key = two element symbols in alphabetical order joined by - = or # ; moment in debye; neg = the delta-minus atom; src = where the number comes from; est = true means a placeholder estimate (no experimental bond moment available).

problems.name: water
problems.note: The bent shape keeps the two O–H bond dipoles from cancelling.

problems.name: ammonia
problems.note: The three N–H bond dipoles all tilt toward N, so they add up along the molecule's axis.

problems.name: hydrogen chloride
problems.note: With only one bond, the bond dipole is the molecular dipole.

problems.name: carbon dioxide
problems.note: Two polar C=O bonds point in exactly opposite directions and cancel.

problems.name: carbon tetrachloride
problems.note: Four identical polar bonds arranged tetrahedrally cancel.

problems.name: carbon tetrafluoride
problems.note: Very polar C–F bonds, but the tetrahedral shape makes them cancel.

problems.name: boron trichloride
problems.note: Three B–Cl dipoles 120° apart in a plane cancel.

problems.name: silicon tetrachloride
problems.note: Tetrahedral, like CCl4: the bond dipoles cancel.

problems.name: silane
problems.note: The Si–H bonds are nonpolar, and the shape is symmetric too.

problems.name: hydrogen cyanide
problems.note: Linear, but the two ends are different: the C≡N dipole is not cancelled.

problems.name: carbon disulfide
problems.note: The C=S bonds are nonpolar, and the linear shape is symmetric.

problems.name: sulfur dioxide
problems.note: The lone pair on S bends the molecule, so the S=O dipoles add instead of cancelling.

problems.name: sulfur trioxide
problems.note: Trigonal planar with three equal S=O bonds: they cancel.

problems.name: phosphorus trichloride
problems.note: The lone pair on P makes the molecule pyramidal, so the P–Cl dipoles don't cancel.

problems.name: phosphorus pentachloride
problems.note: Trigonal bipyramidal: the axial pair and the equatorial three each cancel.

problems.name: nitrogen trifluoride
problems.note: Pyramidal like NH3, so it is polar. The dipole is small because the lone pair on N works against the N–F bond dipoles.

problems.name: oxygen difluoride
problems.note: Bent like water, so the O–F dipoles don't cancel.

problems.name: sulfur dichloride
problems.note: Bent: the two S–Cl dipoles add.

problems.name: sulfur hexafluoride
problems.note: Octahedral: every S–F dipole has a partner pointing the opposite way.

problems.name: xenon difluoride
problems.note: Three lone pairs sit around the middle; the two F atoms are opposite each other, so the dipoles cancel.

problems.name: xenon tetrafluoride
problems.note: Square planar: the four Xe–F dipoles cancel in pairs.

problems.name: phosgene
problems.note: Trigonal planar, but with two kinds of bonds, the dipoles don't cancel.

problems.name: thionyl chloride
problems.note: The lone pair on S makes the molecule pyramidal, and the bonds are not all the same.

problems.name: sulfur tetrafluoride
problems.note: Seesaw: the two axial S–F dipoles cancel, but the two equatorial ones add.

problems.name: chlorine trifluoride
problems.note: T-shaped: the two axial Cl–F dipoles cancel, leaving the equatorial one.

problems.name: bromine pentafluoride
problems.note: Square pyramidal: the four basal Br–F dipoles cancel in the plane, leaving the axial one.

problems.name: methane
problems.note: C–H bonds are nonpolar, and the tetrahedral shape is symmetric.

problems.name: ethane
problems.note: Only C–C and C–H bonds: a hydrocarbon is nonpolar.

problems.name: ethylene (ethene)
problems.note: Only nonpolar bonds.

problems.name: acetylene (ethyne)
problems.note: Only nonpolar bonds, in a straight line.

problems.name: chloromethane
problems.note: One polar C–Cl bond with nothing to cancel it.

problems.name: fluoromethane
problems.note: One polar C–F bond with nothing to cancel it.

problems.name: formaldehyde
problems.note: The C=O dipole is large and nothing cancels it.

problems.name: methanol
problems.note: C–O and O–H dipoles at a bent oxygen add together.

problems.name: dichloromethane
problems.note: Two C–Cl dipoles in a tetrahedron point partly the same way, so they don't cancel.

problems.name: chloroform
problems.note: Three C–Cl dipoles partly cancel, leaving a net dipole toward the chlorines.

problems.name: ethanol
problems.note: The polar C–O–H end makes the molecule polar.

problems.name: dimethyl ether
problems.note: The C–O–C angle is bent, so the two C–O dipoles add.

problems.name: methylamine
problems.note: Pyramidal nitrogen: the N–H and C–N dipoles add.

problems.name: acetonitrile
problems.note: The C≡N bond dipole is one of the largest; nothing cancels it.

problems.name: acetaldehyde
problems.note: The C=O dipole dominates.

problems.name: acetone
problems.note: The C=O dipole dominates; the two methyl groups are nonpolar.

problems.name: formic acid
problems.note: Several polar bonds pointing in different directions partly cancel.

problems.name: acetic acid
problems.note: The polar COOH group makes the molecule polar.

problems.name: cis-1,2-dichloroethylene
problems.note: Both chlorines are on the same side, so the C–Cl dipoles add.

problems.name: trans-1,2-dichloroethylene
problems.note: Same bonds as the cis isomer, but the chlorines are on opposite sides: the dipoles cancel.

problems.name: 1,1-dichloroethylene
problems.note: Both chlorines on one carbon: their dipoles add.

problems.name: benzene
problems.note: Only nonpolar bonds, in a flat symmetric ring.

problems.name: chlorobenzene
problems.note: One polar C–Cl bond on the ring, with nothing to cancel it.

problems.name: 1,4-dichlorobenzene
problems.note: The two C–Cl dipoles are on opposite sides of the ring and cancel.
